newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strikes disrupt French air traffic and hospitals.
newsitem.headline: Strikes disrupt French air traffic and hospitals.

text.p: A strike by cockpit crews halted 60 percent of flights at British Airways' French units TAT and Air Liberte on Friday, management said in a statement.

It said that TAT, a domestic airline, would maintain 68 of its 190 scheduled flights, while Air Liberte, which flies internationally, guaranteed 30 of its 60 flights and would operate all long-haul flights.

Pilots and flight engineers, protesting over pay and conditions which they say will be affected by a merger of the two airlines, have decided to indefinitely extend the strike, which began on Wednesday. It had been due to end at noon (1000 GMT) on Friday.
Unions have urged management to negotiate and say they will continue their strike until they win concessions.
Management said that ground staff had returned to work.
Marc Rochet, chairman of the two units, has rejected demands for reforms which he said would raise costs by 18 percent.

Junior hospital doctors, in their fifth week of a stoppage over government plans to cut health spending, vowed to continue their movement, although yet another teaching hospital, in the southwestern city of Toulouse, voted to return to work.
According to the unions, 19 out of 26 teaching hospitals were still on strike, while the government put the figure at 16.

Representatives of the strikers, protesting against state plans to fine doctors exceeding pre-set spending targets in order to plug a gaping welfare deficit, resumed talks with aides of Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot after both sides said some progress was made on the dispute.
The strikers have called a protest march in Paris on Sunday and a new "health blackout" day, in which they ask other doctors to join them in giving only emergency care, on Monday.
The doctors' dispute is testing the conservative government's determination to cut public deficits to qualify for the European Union's planned single currency in 1999.
